rv.q: What makes this musical so seriously smart is the way that some of the most beloved songs from Morissette's iconic album come right out of the dramatic content, rather than being slapped on top of a wobbly book scene.
The overhauled version that opened on Thursday at the Broadhurst Theater is fully in focus: clear in its priorities, rich in character, sincere without syrup, rousing and real.
It is, indisputably, too much and that too muchness is what makes it so watchable.
The show succeeds in finding fresh emotional contexts for Ms. Morissette's songs while creating a compelling family drama that feels authentically contemporary.
Jagged Little Pill is a flawed but affecting show that uses Morissette's songs to explore issues of sexual assault, addiction and family dysfunction with surprising depth.
Critics have called it 'over-stuffed' and 'overwrought ... but ultimately affecting.'
The musical is packed with tremendous performances and gorgeous vocals, but the story feels forced and the integration of Morissette's songs is often clunky.
The aggressive bid for now-ness is both a blessing and a burden in this overwrought, overstuffed but ultimately affecting show.
It's advice that the creators of this ambitious but frustratingly diffuse show seem to have taken a little too seriously.
Why, you want to howl at the stage, cannot these characters just be real?

I could go on about the soapy predictability of “Jagged Little Pill,” which had its official opening Thursday at the Broadhurst Theatre, with much of the cast intact from its 2018 premiere at Theater in Cambridge, Mass., where Paulus is artistic director.
Me, I found it leaden with earnestness.
The recurrent thoughts watching Jagged Little Pill are: Oh, they’re going there, and oh, they’re really going there, and wow, they went there and did it so well.

"Jagged Little Pill" is no blast-from-the-past jukebox musical but an urgent, rock-driven slice of modern life that tackles nearly every issue of the day: sexual identity, opioid addiction, racial tension, rape.
It is an emotionally rich, beautifully enacted evocation of the conflicting ironies of contemporary life.
It could be said—and will be right here and now—that with Jagged Little Pill Paulus and Cody are contriving a bit too much.
The musical, which opened tonight at the Broadhurst Theatre, is, like the album, surpassingly excellent, if also slightly flawed.
Jagged Little Pill is, indeed, messy: chaotic, complex, overstuffed, way ambitious, and savagely emotional.
As its name has always so annoyingly suggested, Jagged Little Pill is that essential bitter medicine that — despite our jaded impulses — must be swallowed and enjoyed so we can be cured.
Patten (whose DNA was clearly spliced from Laurie Metcalf and Bebe Neuwirth) is an instant star.

Jagged Little Pill can’t resist polishing itself and smoothing out every one of its prickly shards, reducing each microcosmic social issue to a future anecdote recalled at the holidays, told by one big happy family.
Never has a more angst-ridden musical opened on Broadway.
The overstimulating production doesn’t help center an already wildly unfocused script.
That's why it's so disappointing that this stage version mummifies that music in the toilet paper of its book.
Get your ass in this seat and join the revolution!

Jagged Little Pill, the new musical opening on Broadway tonight, ingeniously seizes on the dynamics that made the album divisive and wrests them into an explosive and shattering portrait of American suburbia.

Gooding's songs with Cipriano -- "Ironic," "Head Over Feet" and "That I Would be Good," are sweetly evocative of teenage life and love and come closest to fulfilling the promise of this appealing mess of a musical.
Despite the reservations this reviewer has about the new musical, bookwriter Diablo Cody and director Diane Paulus deserve abundant praise.
That doesn't save JLP from a bit of Mamma Mia-itis, which is what happens when a story is meant to frame a song list.
A dose of Jagged Little Pill delivers desirable jolts to the head and heart thanks to vibrant performances and hits, but this Pill also produces unwanted side effects.
So, yeah, there are a lot of plates in the air, and despite the work of pros such as director Diane Paulus (Waitress, Pippin), it all winds up feeling pretty overwrought.
It’s a significant element here, in a musical that begs us to see the obviousness of who we have become.
